q: A district office wants to deliver a certificate service online, but the records that must be checked before issuing the certificate exist only as paper registers. Why is digitization of those legacy registers a prerequisite for the online service?

opts.A: Because the online workflow cannot verify an application against a record that the software cannot read or search
opts.B: Because the law does not allow paper registers to be retained once a service is offered online
opts.C: Because scanning reduces the physical storage cost of the registers
opts.D: Because digitized registers automatically satisfy the department's data protection obligations

exp: An online service is only end-to-end if the back-end verification step is also electronic; as long as the authoritative record is a paper register, a clerk still has to pull the volume by hand and the service is merely a digital front-end. Reduced storage cost is a side benefit, not the reason the service depends on digitization.

q: In a records digitization programme, what does a 'day-forward' approach mean?

opts.A: All existing records are converted first, and only then is the new system switched on
opts.B: Only records created from the cut-over date onward are captured electronically, with the older backlog handled as a separate exercise
opts.C: Records are re-scanned every day to keep a fresh copy
opts.D: Only the records of the current financial year are retained and the rest are destroyed

exp: Day-forward capture starts the electronic record from a chosen date so that new business is born digital immediately, while the historical backlog is converted on its own timeline or on demand. Converting everything before go-live is the opposite, backlog-first approach, and it usually delays the project far longer.

q: During digitization of departmental files, why is metadata captured for each scanned document in addition to the page images?

opts.A: It compresses the image so the file occupies less disk space
opts.B: It encrypts the document so that only authorised officers can open it
opts.C: It supplies the indexing attributes — such as file number, subject, date and office — by which the document can later be searched and retrieved
opts.D: It guarantees that the scan is a legally admissible copy of the original

exp: A repository of un-indexed page images is effectively unsearchable, so capture of descriptive metadata is what turns a pile of scans into a retrievable record set. Compression and encryption are separate processing steps and neither depends on metadata.

q: Two departments each digitize their records but define the same field differently — one stores a citizen's name as a single field, the other as first and last name, and their date formats differ. What is the main consequence for e-governance?

opts.A: The scanned images will be of unequal resolution
opts.B: The two datasets cannot be reliably exchanged or matched without a costly reconciliation, which is exactly what common data standards exist to prevent
opts.C: Each department will need a separate scanner model
opts.D: The records will lose their legal validity in both departments

exp: Agreed data standards fix the structure, format and meaning of shared elements so that data captured in one department is intelligible to another; without them every inter-departmental exchange needs bespoke mapping and produces matching errors. Image resolution and scanner choice are capture concerns unrelated to field definitions.

q: What does applying OCR to a scanned page add that plain scanning alone does not provide?

opts.A: A machine-readable text layer that makes the content searchable
opts.B: A higher optical resolution for the scanned image
opts.C: A digital signature attesting to the document's authenticity
opts.D: Automatic removal of duplicate pages from the batch

exp: A scan produces only a picture of the page; optical character recognition interprets the shapes as characters and stores the recognised text, so full-text search and data extraction become possible. Resolution is fixed at capture time and is not changed by OCR, and signing is an entirely separate step.

q: Which capability is characteristic of a document management system rather than of an ordinary shared network folder?

opts.A: Allowing several users to open the same file at once
opts.C: Maintaining version history and a check-in/check-out and access-control regime over each document
opts.D: Providing a larger amount of disk space

exp: A document management system adds controlled custody over the document lifecycle — versioning, check-in/check-out to prevent conflicting edits, retention rules and per-document permissions — on top of mere storage. A shared folder gives directories and space but no managed version history.

q: Before the production cut-over of a legacy-to-new-system data migration, why is a trial or dry-run migration into a test environment normally carried out?

opts.A: To increase the transfer speed of the final migration run
opts.B: To let the vendor bill for an additional phase of work
opts.C: To make the legacy system read-only
opts.D: To surface transformation errors, rejected records and reconciliation mismatches while there is still time to correct them

exp: A dry run exercises the full extract-transform-load path on real data and produces the error and reconciliation reports that reveal bad mappings and dirty source records before go-live. It is a rehearsal for correctness, not a performance tuning exercise.

q: After migrating records from a legacy application to a new one, which check most directly establishes that no data was silently lost or altered in transit?

opts.A: Confirming that the new application's screens load without errors
opts.B: Reconciling record counts and control totals of key fields between source and target, plus sample-level field comparison
opts.C: Confirming that the migration job finished without an operating-system error
opts.D: Asking users whether the new system feels faster than the old one

exp: Counts and control totals compared on both sides, backed by row-level sampling, are what actually prove completeness and fidelity of a migration. A job that exits cleanly can still have dropped rejected rows to a log, which is precisely how silent migration loss happens.
